01 • NW
Process over outcome
I judge my work by the parts I control — preparation, discipline, honest effort — not by the scoreboard. It is an idea I borrow from the Bhagavad Gita: do your duty well, and hold the result loosely.
02 • NE
Intellectual honesty
I treat every backtest as guilty until proven innocent. The work I am proudest of is not a winning strategy — it is the documented graveyard of my own ideas that did not survive testing.
03 • SW
A cross-cultural lens
Six years of Mandarin and a childhood spent traveling taught me to question my assumptions and read a situation from more than one angle before acting on it.
04 • SE
An athlete's discipline
Wrestling, distance running, and trading taught me the same lesson in three arenas: define the edge, manage the risk, and trust that small, repeated improvements compound.
02 • JOURNEY
How the methodology was earned.
Every part of the process I trust today exists because an earlier, prettier version of it failed me first. Step through it.

Automated Strategy Research Pipeline
Optuna-Screener
A Python pipeline that discovers, optimizes, and validates strategies on real market data and answers one question honestly: does this work on data it has never seen?
THE PROBLEM
Optimization is the easy part and the dangerous part. A search powerful enough to find an edge is powerful enough to fit noise — so the pipeline is built around the holdout, not the optimizer.

APPROACH
Strategy-file mode: drop in any strategy with entry/exit functions; it computes indicators, optimizes tunable params with walk-forward, stress-tests, and reports on a 25% holdout the optimizer never touched.
Discovery mode: describe a concept in plain English and it searches thousands of indicator / exit / regime combinations.
v3.0 ensemble: 6 structurally distinct strategies combined by risk-parity weighting under a volatility-regime overlay, validated through per-strategy CPCV, portfolio-level CPCV, and walk-forward weighting.

WHAT I LEARNED
A research tool should make it easy to disprove yourself. The honest headline number comes from the data the search was forbidden to touch.
HONEST LIMITATIONS
It is a research and screening tool, not a turnkey trading system — surviving the pipeline earns a candidate a paper deployment, nothing more.

WHERE THE DISCIPLINE STARTED
Automated 0DTE Options Bots
algorithmic-options-trading-system
Automated 0DTE options strategies on SPY / QQQ / SPX, built on the Option Alpha no-code platform and run on a $125K paper portfolio. Three bots, with VIX filters, entry windows, position caps, and a mandatory time-exit.
PAPER • SMALL SAMPLE
Reported paper results (Feb 2026): about +$16,000 (≈ +12.8% on the paper account) across 118 closed trades, with under 3% max drawdown.
HONEST FRAMING
I include this on purpose, framed honestly. These are paper, small-sample numbers with the signature of a short-volatility profile — the kind of result that looks perfect right up until a tail event erases it. It is not a proven edge. It is the experiment that taught me about tail risk and overfitting, and it is exactly why I built the guilty-until-proven-innocent methodology behind everything above.
SUPPORTING WORK
Tools, pipelines, automation.
Hedge-fund
A Dockerized, tested Python project exploring an automated, multi-agent 'AI hedge fund' workflow. Where it builds on an open-source framework, attribution belongs in the write-up.
Data-Scraper
An 82-file Python data pipeline on a clean adapter pattern (Apify, CSV) with scheduled runs and a weekly email digest — a straightforward data-engineering example.
Options-claw
A tiered automation tool for options workflows: webhooks, then Playwright browser automation, then computer-use — escalating only as far as a task requires.
Content-automation-engine
A social-media content-automation system with real infrastructure — Grafana, a database, migrations. The architecture is the point, not the file count.

I grew up watching my father trade and took away one lesson early: results are a byproduct of process — define your edge, manage your risk, and stay level-headed when the noise gets loud. I've spent the last few years turning that instinct into real work: algorithmic strategies on QuantConnect, a research pipeline that stress-tests ideas until most of them break, and a habit of documenting both what survived and what didn't.Away from the screen I run cross country, wrestle, study Mandarin, and shoot photography and drone film. The same temperament runs through all of it — and a quieter thread of moral philosophy runs underneath, shaping how I think about the systems I build.On methodI read moral philosophy and let it shape how I engineer. Mengzi taught me that judgment is cultivated, not innate. The Gita taught me to act with discipline and detach from the result. Mill keeps me weighing consequences and staying open to being wrong; Hegel frames engineering as the reconciliation of competing constraints; the Dhammapada treats a well-directed mind as a technical asset. None of it is decoration — it is why I care whether the systems I build are honest about their limits.JACK’S COMPASS — IT POINTS TO WHAT YOU WANT MOST• , PIRATES OF THE CARIBBEAN01 • NWProcess over outcomeI judge my work by the parts I control — preparation, discipline, honest effort — not by the scoreboard. It is an idea I borrow from the Bhagavad Gita: do your duty well, and hold the result loosely.02 • NEIntellectual honestyI treat every backtest as guilty until proven innocent. The work I am proudest of is not a winning strategy — it is the documented graveyard of my own ideas that did not survive testing.03 • SWA cross-cultural lensSix years of Mandarin and a childhood spent traveling taught me to question my assumptions and read a situation from more than one angle before acting on it.04 • SEAn athlete's disciplineWrestling, distance running, and trading taught me the same lesson in three arenas: define the edge, manage the risk, and trust that small, repeated improvements compound.02 • JourneyHow the methodology was earned.Every part of the process I trust today exists because an earlier, prettier version of it failed me first. secText.about:
01 • ABOUT
A builder of quantitative systems.
I'm Aryan Sharma, a high-school student in the Washington, D.C. area who builds and validates quantitative trading systems. I grew up watching my father trade and took away one lesson early: results are a byproduct of process — define your edge, manage your risk, and stay level-headed when the noise gets loud. I've spent the last few years turning that instinct into real work: algorithmic strategies on QuantConnect, a research pipeline that stress-tests ideas until most of them break, and a habit of documenting both what survived and what didn't.
Away from the screen I run cross country, wrestle, study Mandarin, and shoot photography and drone film. The same temperament runs through all of it — and a quieter thread of moral philosophy runs underneath, shaping how I think about the systems I build.
ON METHOD
I read moral philosophy and let it shape how I engineer. Mengzi taught me that judgment is cultivated, not innate. The Gita taught me to act with discipline and detach from the result. Mill keeps me weighing consequences and staying open to being wrong; Hegel frames engineering as the reconciliation of competing constraints; the Dhammapada treats a well-directed mind as a technical asset. None of it is decoration — it is why I care whether the systems I build are honest about their limits.
JACK’S COMPASS — IT POINTS TO WHAT YOU WANT MOST• 
,
PIRATES OF THE CARIBBEAN
01 • NW
Process over outcome
I judge my work by the parts I control — preparation, discipline, honest effort — not by the scoreboard. It is an idea I borrow from the Bhagavad Gita: do your duty well, and hold the result loosely.
02 • NE
Intellectual honesty
I treat every backtest as guilty until proven innocent. The work I am proudest of is not a winning strategy — it is the documented graveyard of my own ideas that did not survive testing.
03 • SW
A cross-cultural lens
Six years of Mandarin and a childhood spent traveling taught me to question my assumptions and read a situation from more than one angle before acting on it.
04 • SE
An athlete's discipline
Wrestling, distance running, and trading taught me the same lesson in three arenas: define the edge, manage the risk, and trust that small, repeated improvements compound.

05 • FLAGSHIP · 161 FILES
Automated Strategy Research Pipeline
Optuna-Screener
A Python pipeline that discovers, optimizes, and validates strategies on real market data and answers one question honestly: does this work on data it has never seen?
THE PROBLEM
Optimization is the easy part and the dangerous part. A search powerful enough to find an edge is powerful enough to fit noise — so the pipeline is built around the holdout, not the optimizer.
FIG. 2 • OPTUNA-SCREENER • 6 STAGES • 1 BRANCH

APPROACH
Strategy-file mode: drop in any strategy with entry/exit functions; it computes indicators, optimizes tunable params with walk-forward, stress-tests, and reports on a 25% holdout the optimizer never touched.
Discovery mode: describe a concept in plain English and it searches thousands of indicator / exit / regime combinations.
v3.0 ensemble: 6 structurally distinct strategies combined by risk-parity weighting under a volatility-regime overlay, validated through per-strategy CPCV, portfolio-level CPCV, and walk-forward weighting.
MONTE-CARLO SHUFFLES
3,000+
trade-sequence resampling
OUT-OF-SAMPLE HOLDOUT
25%
optimizer never sees it
TARGET CPCV SHARPE
1.0–1.5
anything > 2.0 is a red flag
WHAT I LEARNED
A research tool should make it easy to disprove yourself. The honest headline number comes from the data the search was forbidden to touch.
HONEST LIMITATIONS
It is a research and screening tool, not a turnkey trading system — surviving the pipeline earns a candidate a paper deployment, nothing more.

WHERE THE DISCIPLINE STARTED
Automated 0DTE Options Bots
algorithmic-options-trading-system
Automated 0DTE options strategies on SPY / QQQ / SPX, built on the Option Alpha no-code platform and run on a $125K paper portfolio. Three bots, with VIX filters, entry windows, position caps, and a mandatory time-exit.
PAPER • SMALL SAMPLE
Reported paper results (Feb 2026): about +$16,000 (≈ +12.8% on the paper account) across 118 closed trades, with under 3% max drawdown.
HONEST FRAMING
I include this on purpose, framed honestly. These are paper, small-sample numbers with the signature of a short-volatility profile — the kind of result that looks perfect right up until a tail event erases it. It is not a proven edge. It is the experiment that taught me about tail risk and overfitting, and it is exactly why I built the guilty-until-proven-innocent methodology behind everything above.
SUPPORTING WORK
Tools, pipelines, automation.

A Dockerized, tested Python project exploring an automated, multi-agent 'AI hedge fund' workflow. Where it builds on an open-source framework, attribution belongs in the write-up.

An 82-file Python data pipeline on a clean adapter pattern (Apify, CSV) with scheduled runs and a weekly email digest — a straightforward data-engineering example.
Options-claw
A tiered automation tool for options workflows: webhooks, then Playwright browser automation, then computer-use — escalating only as far as a task requires.
Content-automation-engine
A social-media content-automation system with real infrastructure — Grafana, a database, migrations. The architecture is the point, not the file count.

secText.principles:
THE MAP OF THE PRINCIPLES
10 • PRINCIPLES
A small philosophy of work.
Five ideas I actually use when I build. The names are sources, not decoration.
THE MARAUDER’S MAP• 
,
HARRY POTTER
YOU
01
Cultivate judgment
Good judgment is trained, not issued at birth. I treat skill and temperament like mileage or lifts — built slowly, on purpose.
AFTER MENGZI
YOU
02
Act, then release the result
Do the work well and hold the outcome loosely. The scoreboard is feedback, not a verdict on the process that produced it.
AFTER THE BHAGAVAD GITA
YOU
03
Weigh the consequences
Systems that touch people carry downstream effects. Risk is partly a moral category — and staying open to being wrong is part of the design.
AFTER J. S. MILL
YOU
04
Synthesize the constraints
Engineering is the reconciliation of competing demands — speed against cost, ambition against honesty. Progress comes through that tension, not around it.
AFTER HEGEL
YOU
05
Attend carefully
A disciplined, well-directed mind is a technical asset. Most failures I have seen were failures of attention before they were failures of math.

01 • ABOUT
A builder of quantitative systems.
I'm Aryan Sharma, a high-school student in the Washington, D.C. area who builds and validates quantitative trading systems. I grew up watching my father trade and took away one lesson early: results are a byproduct of process — define your edge, manage your risk, and stay level-headed when the noise gets loud. I've spent the last few years turning that instinct into real work: algorithmic strategies on QuantConnect, a research pipeline that stress-tests ideas until most of them break, and a habit of documenting both what survived and what didn't.
Away from the screen I run cross country, wrestle, study Mandarin, and shoot photography and drone film. The same temperament runs through all of it — and a quieter thread of moral philosophy runs underneath, shaping how I think about the systems I build.
ON METHOD
I read moral philosophy and let it shape how I engineer. Mengzi taught me that judgment is cultivated, not innate. The Gita taught me to act with discipline and detach from the result. Mill keeps me weighing consequences and staying open to being wrong; Hegel frames engineering as the reconciliation of competing constraints; the Dhammapada treats a well-directed mind as a technical asset. None of it is decoration — it is why I care whether the systems I build are honest about their limits.
JACK’S COMPASS — IT POINTS TO WHAT YOU WANT MOST

Process over outcome
I judge my work by the parts I control — preparation, discipline, honest effort — not by the scoreboard. It is an idea I borrow from the Bhagavad Gita: do your duty well, and hold the result loosely.
02 • NE
Intellectual honesty
I treat every backtest as guilty until proven innocent. The work I am proudest of is not a winning strategy — it is the documented graveyard of my own ideas that did not survive testing.
03 • SW
A cross-cultural lens
Six years of Mandarin and a childhood spent traveling taught me to question my assumptions and read a situation from more than one angle before acting on it.
04 • SE
An athlete's discipline
Wrestling, distance running, and trading taught me the same lesson in three arenas: define the edge, manage the risk, and trust that small, repeated improvements compound.
02 • JOURNEY
How the methodology was earned.
Every part of the process I trust today exists because an earlier, prettier version of it failed me first. Step through it.

Automated Strategy Research Pipeline
Optuna-Screener
A Python pipeline that discovers, optimizes, and validates strategies on real market data and answers one question honestly: does this work on data it has never seen?
THE PROBLEM
Optimization is the easy part and the dangerous part. A search powerful enough to find an edge is powerful enough to fit noise — so the pipeline is built around the holdout, not the optimizer.

APPROACH
Strategy-file mode: drop in any strategy with entry/exit functions; it computes indicators, optimizes tunable params with walk-forward, stress-tests, and reports on a 25% holdout the optimizer never touched.
Discovery mode: describe a concept in plain English and it searches thousands of indicator / exit / regime combinations.
v3.0 ensemble: 6 structurally distinct strategies combined by risk-parity weighting under a volatility-regime overlay, validated through per-strategy CPCV, portfolio-level CPCV, and walk-forward weighting.

WHAT I LEARNED
A research tool should make it easy to disprove yourself. The honest headline number comes from the data the search was forbidden to touch.
HONEST LIMITATIONS
It is a research and screening tool, not a turnkey trading system — surviving the pipeline earns a candidate a paper deployment, nothing more.

HONEST FRAMING

It is the experiment that taught me about tail risk and overfitting, and it is exactly why I built the guilty-until-proven-innocent methodology behind everything above.

Cultivate judgment
Good judgment is trained, not issued at birth. I treat skill and temperament like mileage or lifts — built slowly, on purpose.

YOU
02
Act, then release the result
Do the work well and hold the outcome loosely. The scoreboard is feedback, not a verdict on the process that produced it.
AFTER THE BHAGAVAD GITA
YOU
03
Weigh the consequences
Systems that touch people carry downstream effects. Risk is partly a moral category — and staying open to being wrong is part of the design.
AFTER J. S. MILL
YOU
04
Synthesize the constraints
Engineering is the reconciliation of competing demands — speed against cost, ambition against honesty. Progress comes through that tension, not around it.
AFTER HEGEL
YOU
05
Attend carefully
A disciplined, well-directed mind is a technical asset. Most failures I have seen were failures of attention before they were failures of math.

secText.about:
01 • ABOUT
A builder of quantitative systems.
I'm Aryan Sharma, a high-school student in the Washington, D.C. area who builds and validates quantitative trading systems. I grew up watching my father trade and took away one lesson early: results are a byproduct of process — define your edge, manage your risk, and stay level-headed when the noise gets loud. I've spent the last few years turning that instinct into real work: algorithmic strategies on QuantConnect, a research pipeline that stress-tests ideas until most of them break, and a habit of documenting both what survived and what didn't.
Away from the screen I run cross country, wrestle, study Mandarin, and shoot photography and drone film. The same temperament runs through all of it — and a quieter thread of moral philosophy runs underneath, shaping how I think about the systems I build.
ON METHOD
I read moral philosophy and let it shape how I engineer. Mengzi taught me that judgment is cultivated, not innate. The Gita taught me to act with discipline and detach from the result. Mill keeps me weighing consequences and staying open to being wrong; Hegel frames engineering as the reconciliation of competing constraints; the Dhammapada treats a well-directed mind as a technical asset. None of it is decoration — it is why I care whether the systems I build are honest about their limits.
JACK’S COMPASS — IT POINTS TO WHAT YOU WANT MOST
,
PIRATES OF THE CARIBBEAN
01 • NW
Process over outcome
I judge my work by the parts I control — preparation, discipline, honest effort — not by the scoreboard. It is an idea I borrow from the Bhagavad Gita: do your duty well, and hold the result loosely.
02 • NE
Intellectual honesty
I treat every backtest as guilty until proven innocent. The work I am proudest of is not a winning strategy — it is the documented graveyard of my own ideas that did not survive testing.
03 • SW
A cross-cultural lens
Six years of Mandarin and a childhood spent traveling taught me to question my assumptions and read a situation from more than one angle before acting on it.
04 • SE
An athlete's discipline
Wrestling, distance running, and trading taught me the same lesson in three arenas: define the edge, manage the risk, and trust that small, repeated improvements compound.

Optuna-Screener
A Python pipeline that discovers, optimizes, and validates strategies on real market data and answers one question honestly: does this work on data it has never seen?
THE PROBLEM
Optimization is the easy part and the dangerous part. A search powerful enough to find an edge is powerful enough to fit noise — so the pipeline is built around the holdout, not the optimizer.

APPROACH
Strategy-file mode: drop in any strategy with entry/exit functions; it computes indicators, optimizes tunable params with walk-forward, stress-tests, and reports on a 25% holdout the optimizer never touched.
Discovery mode: describe a concept in plain English and it searches thousands of indicator / exit / regime combinations.
v3.0 ensemble: 6 structurally distinct strategies combined by risk-parity weighting under a volatility-regime overlay, validated through per-strategy CPCV, portfolio-level CPCV, and walk-forward weighting.

WHAT I LEARNED
A research tool should make it easy to disprove yourself. The honest headline number comes from the data the search was forbidden to touch.
HONEST LIMITATIONS
It is a research and screening tool, not a turnkey trading system — surviving the pipeline earns a candidate a paper deployment, nothing more.

PAPER • SMALL SAMPLE
Reported paper results (Feb 2026): about +$16,000 (≈ +12.8% on the paper account) across 118 closed trades, with under 3% max drawdown.
HONEST FRAMING
I include this on purpose, framed honestly. These are paper, small-sample numbers with the signature of a short-volatility profile — the kind of result that looks perfect right up until a tail event erases it. It is not a proven edge. It is the experiment that taught me about tail risk and overfitting, and it is exactly why I built the guilty-until-proven-innocent methodology behind everything above.

THE MAP OF THE PRINCIPLES
10 • PRINCIPLES
A small philosophy of work.
Five ideas I actually use when I build. The names are sources, not decoration.
THE MARAUDER’S MAP
,
HARRY POTTER
YOU
01
Cultivate judgment
Good judgment is trained, not issued at birth. I treat skill and temperament like mileage or lifts — built slowly, on purpose.
AFTER MENGZI
YOU
02
Act, then release the result
Do the work well and hold the outcome loosely. The scoreboard is feedback, not a verdict on the process that produced it.
AFTER THE BHAGAVAD GITA
YOU
03
Weigh the consequences
Systems that touch people carry downstream effects. Risk is partly a moral category — and staying open to being wrong is part of the design.
AFTER J. S. MILL
YOU
04
Synthesize the constraints
Engineering is the reconciliation of competing demands — speed against cost, ambition against honesty. Progress comes through that tension, not around it.
AFTER HEGEL
YOU
05
Attend carefully
A disciplined, well-directed mind is a technical asset. Most failures I have seen were failures of attention before they were failures of math.
AFTER THE DHAMMAPADA

secAll.about: 01 • AboutA builder of quantitative systems.JACK’S COMPASS — IT POINTS TO WHAT YOU WANT MOST• , PIRATES OF THE CARIBBEANI'm Aryan Sharma, a high-school student in the Washington, D.C. area who builds and validates quantitative trading systems. I grew up watching my father trade and took away one lesson early: results are a byproduct of process — define your edge, manage your risk, and stay level-headed when the noise gets loud. I've spent the last few years turning that instinct into real work: algorithmic strategies on QuantConnect, a research pipeline that stress-tests ideas until most of them break, and a habit of documenting both what survived and what didn't.Away from the screen I run cross country, wrestle, study Mandarin, and shoot photography and drone film. The same temperament runs through all of it — and a quieter thread of moral philosophy runs underneath, shaping how I think about the systems I build.On methodI read moral philosophy and let it shape how I engineer. Mengzi taught me that judgment is cultivated, not innate. The Gita taught me to act with discipline and detach from the result. Mill keeps me weighing consequences and staying open to being wrong; Hegel frames engineering as the reconciliation of competing constraints; the Dhammapada treats a well-directed mind as a technical asset. None of it is decoration — it is why I care whether the systems I build are honest about their limits.JACK’S COMPASS — IT POINTS TO WHAT YOU WANT MOST• , PIRATES OF THE CARIBBEAN01 • NWProcess over outcomeI judge my work by the parts I control — preparation, discipline, honest effort — not by the scoreboard. It is an idea I borrow from the Bhagavad Gita: do your duty well, and hold the result loosely.02 • NEIntellectual honestyI treat every backtest as guilty until proven innocent. The work I am proudest of is not a winning strategy — it is the documented graveyard of my own ideas that did not survive testing.03 • SWA cross-cultural lensSix years of Mandarin and a childhood spent traveling taught me to question my assumptions and read a situation from more than one angle before acting on it.04 • SEAn athlete's disciplineWrestling, distance running, and trading taught me the same lesson in three arenas: define the edge, manage the risk, and trust that small, repeated improvements compound.

01 • ABOUT
A builder of quantitative systems.
I'm Aryan Sharma, a high-school student in the Washington, D.C. area who builds and validates quantitative trading systems. I grew up watching my father trade and took away one lesson early: results are a byproduct of process — define your edge, manage your risk, and stay level-headed when the noise gets loud. I've spent the last few years turning that instinct into real work: algorithmic strategies on QuantConnect, a research pipeline that stress-tests ideas until most of them break, and a habit of documenting both what survived and what didn't.
Away from the screen I run cross country, wrestle, study Mandarin, and shoot photography and drone film. The same temperament runs through all of it — and a quieter thread of moral philosophy runs underneath, shaping how I think about the systems I build.
ON METHOD
I read moral philosophy and let it shape how I engineer. Mengzi taught me that judgment is cultivated, not innate. The Gita taught me to act with discipline and detach from the result. Mill keeps me weighing consequences and staying open to being wrong; Hegel frames engineering as the reconciliation of competing constraints; the Dhammapada treats a well-directed mind as a technical asset. None of it is decoration — it is why I care whether the systems I build are honest about their limits.
JACK’S COMPASS — IT POINTS TO WHAT YOU WANT MOST

Process over outcome
I judge my work by the parts I control — preparation, discipline, honest effort — not by the scoreboard. It is an idea I borrow from the Bhagavad Gita: do your duty well, and hold the result loosely.
02 • NE
Intellectual honesty
I treat every backtest as guilty until proven innocent. The work I am proudest of is not a winning strategy — it is the documented graveyard of my own ideas that did not survive testing.

A cross-cultural lens
Six years of Mandarin and a childhood spent traveling taught me to question my assumptions and read a situation from more than one angle before acting on it.
04 • SE
An athlete's discipline
Wrestling, distance running, and trading taught me the same lesson in three arenas: define the edge, manage the risk, and trust that small, repeated improvements compound.

Optuna-Screener
A Python pipeline that discovers, optimizes, and validates strategies on real market data and answers one question honestly: does this work on data it has never seen?
THE PROBLEM
Optimization is the easy part and the dangerous part. A search powerful enough to find an edge is powerful enough to fit noise — so the pipeline is built around the holdout, not the optimizer.

APPROACH
Strategy-file mode: drop in any strategy with entry/exit functions; it computes indicators, optimizes tunable params with walk-forward, stress-tests, and reports on a 25% holdout the optimizer never touched.
Discovery mode: describe a concept in plain English and it searches thousands of indicator / exit / regime combinations.
v3.0 ensemble: 6 structurally distinct strategies combined by risk-parity weighting under a volatility-regime overlay, validated through per-strategy CPCV, portfolio-level CPCV, and walk-forward weighting.

WHAT I LEARNED
A research tool should make it easy to disprove yourself. The honest headline number comes from the data the search was forbidden to touch.
HONEST LIMITATIONS
It is a research and screening tool, not a turnkey trading system — surviving the pipeline earns a candidate a paper deployment, nothing more.

Automated 0DTE Options Bots
algorithmic-options-trading-system
Automated 0DTE options strategies on SPY / QQQ / SPX, built on the Option Alpha no-code platform and run on a $125K paper portfolio. Three bots, with VIX filters, entry windows, position caps, and a mandatory time-exit.
PAPER • SMALL SAMPLE
Reported paper results (Feb 2026): about +$16,000 (≈ +12.8% on the paper account) across 118 closed trades, with under 3% max drawdown.
HONEST FRAMING
I include this on purpose, framed honestly. These are paper, small-sample numbers with the signature of a short-volatility profile — the kind of result that looks perfect right up until a tail event erases it. It is not a proven edge. It is the experiment that taught me about tail risk and overfitting, and it is exactly why I built the guilty-until-proven-innocent methodology behind everything above.
SUPPORTING WORK
Tools, pipelines, automation.

A Dockerized, tested Python project exploring an automated, multi-agent 'AI hedge fund' workflow. Where it builds on an open-source framework, attribution belongs in the write-up.

A tiered automation tool for options workflows: webhooks, then Playwright browser automation, then computer-use — escalating only as far as a task requires.
Content-automation-engine

YOU
01
Cultivate judgment
Good judgment is trained, not issued at birth. I treat skill and temperament like mileage or lifts — built slowly, on purpose.
AFTER MENGZI
YOU
02
Act, then release the result
Do the work well and hold the outcome loosely. The scoreboard is feedback, not a verdict on the process that produced it.
AFTER THE BHAGAVAD GITA
YOU
03
Weigh the consequences
Systems that touch people carry downstream effects. Risk is partly a moral category — and staying open to being wrong is part of the design.
AFTER J. S. MILL
YOU
04
Synthesize the constraints
Engineering is the reconciliation of competing demands — speed against cost, ambition against honesty. Progress comes through that tension, not around it.
AFTER HEGEL
YOU
05
Attend carefully
A disciplined, well-directed mind is a technical asset. Most failures I have seen were failures of attention before they were failures of math.

I grew up watching my father trade and took away one lesson early: results are a byproduct of process — define your edge, manage your risk, and stay level-headed when the noise gets loud. I've spent the last few years turning that instinct into real work: algorithmic strategies on QuantConnect, a research pipeline that stress-tests ideas until most of them break, and a habit of documenting both what survived and what didn't.Away from the screen I run cross country, wrestle, study Mandarin, and shoot photography and drone film. The same temperament runs through all of it — and a quieter thread of moral philosophy runs underneath, shaping how I think about the systems I build.On methodI read moral philosophy and let it shape how I engineer. Mengzi taught me that judgment is cultivated, not innate. The Gita taught me to act with discipline and detach from the result. Mill keeps me weighing consequences and staying open to being wrong; Hegel frames engineering as the reconciliation of competing constraints; the Dhammapada treats a well-directed mind as a technical asset. None of it is decoration — it is why I care whether the systems I build are honest about their limits.JACK’S COMPASS — IT POINTS TO WHAT YOU WANT MOST• , PIRATES OF THE CARIBBEAN01 • NWProcess over outcomeI judge my work by the parts I control — preparation, discipline, honest effort — not by the scoreboard. secText.about:
01 • ABOUT
A builder of quantitative systems.
I'm Aryan Sharma, a high-school student in the Washington, D.C. area who builds and validates quantitative trading systems. I grew up watching my father trade and took away one lesson early: results are a byproduct of process — define your edge, manage your risk, and stay level-headed when the noise gets loud. I've spent the last few years turning that instinct into real work: algorithmic strategies on QuantConnect, a research pipeline that stress-tests ideas until most of them break, and a habit of documenting both what survived and what didn't.
Away from the screen I run cross country, wrestle, study Mandarin, and shoot photography and drone film. The same temperament runs through all of it — and a quieter thread of moral philosophy runs underneath, shaping how I think about the systems I build.
ON METHOD
I read moral philosophy and let it shape how I engineer. Mengzi taught me that judgment is cultivated, not innate. The Gita taught me to act with discipline and detach from the result. Mill keeps me weighing consequences and staying open to being wrong; Hegel frames engineering as the reconciliation of competing constraints; the Dhammapada treats a well-directed mind as a technical asset. None of it is decoration — it is why I care whether the systems I build are honest about their limits.
JACK’S COMPASS — IT POINTS TO WHAT YOU WANT MOST
,
PIRATES OF THE CARIBBEAN
01 • NW
Process over outcome
I judge my work by the parts I control — preparation, discipline, honest effort — not by the scoreboard. It is an idea I borrow from the Bhagavad Gita: do your duty well, and hold the result loosely.
02 • NE
Intellectual honesty
I treat every backtest as guilty until proven innocent. The work I am proudest of is not a winning strategy — it is the documented graveyard of my own ideas that did not survive testing.
03 • SW
A cross-cultural lens
Six years of Mandarin and a childhood spent traveling taught me to question my assumptions and read a situation from more than one angle before acting on it.
04 • SE
An athlete's discipline
Wrestling, distance running, and trading taught me the same lesson in three arenas: define the edge, manage the risk, and trust that small, repeated improvements compound.

05 • FLAGSHIP · 161 FILES
Automated Strategy Research Pipeline
Optuna-Screener
A Python pipeline that discovers, optimizes, and validates strategies on real market data and answers one question honestly: does this work on data it has never seen?
THE PROBLEM
Optimization is the easy part and the dangerous part. A search powerful enough to find an edge is powerful enough to fit noise — so the pipeline is built around the holdout, not the optimizer.
FIG. 2 • OPTUNA-SCREENER • 6 STAGES • 1 BRANCH

RISK-PARITY WEIGHTING • PER-STRATEGY + PORTFOLIO CPCV
APPROACH
Strategy-file mode: drop in any strategy with entry/exit functions; it computes indicators, optimizes tunable params with walk-forward, stress-tests, and reports on a 25% holdout the optimizer never touched.
Discovery mode: describe a concept in plain English and it searches thousands of indicator / exit / regime combinations.
v3.0 ensemble: 6 structurally distinct strategies combined by risk-parity weighting under a volatility-regime overlay, validated through per-strategy CPCV, portfolio-level CPCV, and walk-forward weighting.
MONTE-CARLO SHUFFLES
3,000+
trade-sequence resampling
OUT-OF-SAMPLE HOLDOUT
25%
optimizer never sees it
TARGET CPCV SHARPE
1.0–1.5
anything > 2.0 is a red flag
WHAT I LEARNED
A research tool should make it easy to disprove yourself. The honest headline number comes from the data the search was forbidden to touch.
HONEST LIMITATIONS
It is a research and screening tool, not a turnkey trading system — surviving the pipeline earns a candidate a paper deployment, nothing more.

Automated 0DTE Options Bots
algorithmic-options-trading-system
Automated 0DTE options strategies on SPY / QQQ / SPX, built on the Option Alpha no-code platform and run on a $125K paper portfolio. Three bots, with VIX filters, entry windows, position caps, and a mandatory time-exit.
PAPER • SMALL SAMPLE
Reported paper results (Feb 2026): about +$16,000 (≈ +12.8% on the paper account) across 118 closed trades, with under 3% max drawdown.
HONEST FRAMING
I include this on purpose, framed honestly. These are paper, small-sample numbers with the signature of a short-volatility profile — the kind of result that looks perfect right up until a tail event erases it. It is not a proven edge. It is the experiment that taught me about tail risk and overfitting, and it is exactly why I built the guilty-until-proven-innocent methodology behind everything above.

A tiered automation tool for options workflows: webhooks, then Playwright browser automation, then computer-use — escalating only as far as a task requires.

01 • ABOUT
A builder of quantitative systems.
I'm Aryan Sharma, a high-school student in the Washington, D.C. area who builds and validates quantitative trading systems. I grew up watching my father trade and took away one lesson early: results are a byproduct of process — define your edge, manage your risk, and stay level-headed when the noise gets loud. I've spent the last few years turning that instinct into real work: algorithmic strategies on QuantConnect, a research pipeline that stress-tests ideas until most of them break, and a habit of documenting both what survived and what didn't.
Away from the screen I run cross country, wrestle, study Mandarin, and shoot photography and drone film. The same temperament runs through all of it — and a quieter thread of moral philosophy runs underneath, shaping how I think about the systems I build.
ON METHOD
I read moral philosophy and let it shape how I engineer. Mengzi taught me that judgment is cultivated, not innate. The Gita taught me to act with discipline and detach from the result. Mill keeps me weighing consequences and staying open to being wrong; Hegel frames engineering as the reconciliation of competing constraints; the Dhammapada treats a well-directed mind as a technical asset. None of it is decoration — it is why I care whether the systems I build are honest about their limits.
JACK’S COMPASS — IT POINTS TO WHAT YOU WANT MOST
,
PIRATES OF THE CARIBBEAN
01 • NW
Process over outcome
I judge my work by the parts I control — preparation, discipline, honest effort — not by the scoreboard. It is an idea I borrow from the Bhagavad Gita: do your duty well, and hold the result loosely.
02 • NE
Intellectual honesty
I treat every backtest as guilty until proven innocent. The work I am proudest of is not a winning strategy — it is the documented graveyard of my own ideas that did not survive testing.
03 • SW
A cross-cultural lens
Six years of Mandarin and a childhood spent traveling taught me to question my assumptions and read a situation from more than one angle before acting on it.
04 • SE
An athlete's discipline
Wrestling, distance running, and trading taught me the same lesson in three arenas: define the edge, manage the risk, and trust that small, repeated improvements compound.

Automated Strategy Research Pipeline
Optuna-Screener
A Python pipeline that discovers, optimizes, and validates strategies on real market data and answers one question honestly: does this work on data it has never seen?
THE PROBLEM
Optimization is the easy part and the dangerous part. A search powerful enough to find an edge is powerful enough to fit noise — so the pipeline is built around the holdout, not the optimizer.

APPROACH
Strategy-file mode: drop in any strategy with entry/exit functions; it computes indicators, optimizes tunable params with walk-forward, stress-tests, and reports on a 25% holdout the optimizer never touched.
Discovery mode: describe a concept in plain English and it searches thousands of indicator / exit / regime combinations.
v3.0 ensemble: 6 structurally distinct strategies combined by risk-parity weighting under a volatility-regime overlay, validated through per-strategy CPCV, portfolio-level CPCV, and walk-forward weighting.

WHAT I LEARNED
A research tool should make it easy to disprove yourself. The honest headline number comes from the data the search was forbidden to touch.
HONEST LIMITATIONS
It is a research and screening tool, not a turnkey trading system — surviving the pipeline earns a candidate a paper deployment, nothing more.

Automated 0DTE Options Bots
algorithmic-options-trading-system
Automated 0DTE options strategies on SPY / QQQ / SPX, built on the Option Alpha no-code platform and run on a $125K paper portfolio. Three bots, with VIX filters, entry windows, position caps, and a mandatory time-exit.
PAPER • SMALL SAMPLE
Reported paper results (Feb 2026): about +$16,000 (≈ +12.8% on the paper account) across 118 closed trades, with under 3% max drawdown.
HONEST FRAMING
I include this on purpose, framed honestly. These are paper, small-sample numbers with the signature of a short-volatility profile — the kind of result that looks perfect right up until a tail event erases it. It is not a proven edge. It is the experiment that taught me about tail risk and overfitting, and it is exactly why I built the guilty-until-proven-innocent methodology behind everything above.

YOU
01
Cultivate judgment
Good judgment is trained, not issued at birth. I treat skill and temperament like mileage or lifts — built slowly, on purpose.
AFTER MENGZI
YOU
02
Act, then release the result
Do the work well and hold the outcome loosely. The scoreboard is feedback, not a verdict on the process that produced it.
AFTER THE BHAGAVAD GITA
YOU
03
Weigh the consequences
Systems that touch people carry downstream effects. Risk is partly a moral category — and staying open to being wrong is part of the design.
AFTER J. S. MILL
YOU
04
Synthesize the constraints
Engineering is the reconciliation of competing demands — speed against cost, ambition against honesty. Progress comes through that tension, not around it.
AFTER HEGEL
YOU
05
Attend carefully
A disciplined, well-directed mind is a technical asset. Most failures I have seen were failures of attention before they were failures of math.

secText.about:
01 • ABOUT
A builder of quantitative systems.
I'm Aryan Sharma, a high-school student in the Washington, D.C. area who builds and validates quantitative trading systems. I grew up watching my father trade and took away one lesson early: results are a byproduct of process — define your edge, manage your risk, and stay level-headed when the noise gets loud. I've spent the last few years turning that instinct into real work: algorithmic strategies on QuantConnect, a research pipeline that stress-tests ideas until most of them break, and a habit of documenting both what survived and what didn't.
Away from the screen I run cross country, wrestle, study Mandarin, and shoot photography and drone film. The same temperament runs through all of it — and a quieter thread of moral philosophy runs underneath, shaping how I think about the systems I build.
ON METHOD
I read moral philosophy and let it shape how I engineer. Mengzi taught me that judgment is cultivated, not innate. The Gita taught me to act with discipline and detach from the result. Mill keeps me weighing consequences and staying open to being wrong; Hegel frames engineering as the reconciliation of competing constraints; the Dhammapada treats a well-directed mind as a technical asset. None of it is decoration — it is why I care whether the systems I build are honest about their limits.
JACK’S COMPASS — IT POINTS TO WHAT YOU WANT MOST
,
PIRATES OF THE CARIBBEAN
01 • NW
Process over outcome
I judge my work by the parts I control — preparation, discipline, honest effort — not by the scoreboard. It is an idea I borrow from the Bhagavad Gita: do your duty well, and hold the result loosely.
02 • NE
Intellectual honesty
I treat every backtest as guilty until proven innocent. The work I am proudest of is not a winning strategy — it is the documented graveyard of my own ideas that did not survive testing.
03 • SW
A cross-cultural lens
Six years of Mandarin and a childhood spent traveling taught me to question my assumptions and read a situation from more than one angle before acting on it.
04 • SE
An athlete's discipline
Wrestling, distance running, and trading taught me the same lesson in three arenas: define the edge, manage the risk, and trust that small, repeated improvements compound.

A Python pipeline that discovers, optimizes, and validates strategies on real market data and answers one question honestly: does this work on data it has never seen?
THE PROBLEM
Optimization is the easy part and the dangerous part. A search powerful enough to find an edge is powerful enough to fit noise — so the pipeline is built around the holdout, not the optimizer.

A small philosophy of work.
Five ideas I actually use when I build. The names are sources, not decoration.
THE MARAUDER’S MAP

HARRY POTTER
YOU
01
Cultivate judgment
Good judgment is trained, not issued at birth. I treat skill and temperament like mileage or lifts — built slowly, on purpose.
AFTER MENGZI
YOU
02
Act, then release the result
Do the work well and hold the outcome loosely. The scoreboard is feedback, not a verdict on the process that produced it.
AFTER THE BHAGAVAD GITA
YOU
03
Weigh the consequences
Systems that touch people carry downstream effects. Risk is partly a moral category — and staying open to being wrong is part of the design.
AFTER J. S. MILL
YOU
04
Synthesize the constraints
Engineering is the reconciliation of competing demands — speed against cost, ambition against honesty. Progress comes through that tension, not around it.
AFTER HEGEL
YOU
05
Attend carefully
A disciplined, well-directed mind is a technical asset. Most failures I have seen were failures of attention before they were failures of math.

01 • ABOUT
A builder of quantitative systems.
I'm Aryan Sharma, a high-school student in the Washington, D.C. area who builds and validates quantitative trading systems. I grew up watching my father trade and took away one lesson early: results are a byproduct of process — define your edge, manage your risk, and stay level-headed when the noise gets loud. I've spent the last few years turning that instinct into real work: algorithmic strategies on QuantConnect, a research pipeline that stress-tests ideas until most of them break, and a habit of documenting both what survived and what didn't.
Away from the screen I run cross country, wrestle, study Mandarin, and shoot photography and drone film. The same temperament runs through all of it — and a quieter thread of moral philosophy runs underneath, shaping how I think about the systems I build.
ON METHOD
I read moral philosophy and let it shape how I engineer. Mengzi taught me that judgment is cultivated, not innate. The Gita taught me to act with discipline and detach from the result. Mill keeps me weighing consequences and staying open to being wrong; Hegel frames engineering as the reconciliation of competing constraints; the Dhammapada treats a well-directed mind as a technical asset. None of it is decoration — it is why I care whether the systems I build are honest about their limits.
JACK’S COMPASS — IT POINTS TO WHAT YOU WANT MOST

Process over outcome
I judge my work by the parts I control — preparation, discipline, honest effort — not by the scoreboard. It is an idea I borrow from the Bhagavad Gita: do your duty well, and hold the result loosely.
02 • NE
Intellectual honesty
I treat every backtest as guilty until proven innocent. The work I am proudest of is not a winning strategy — it is the documented graveyard of my own ideas that did not survive testing.

Six years of Mandarin and a childhood spent traveling taught me to question my assumptions and read a situation from more than one angle before acting on it.
04 • SE
An athlete's discipline
Wrestling, distance running, and trading taught me the same lesson in three arenas: define the edge, manage the risk, and trust that small, repeated improvements compound.

Optuna-Screener
A Python pipeline that discovers, optimizes, and validates strategies on real market data and answers one question honestly: does this work on data it has never seen?
THE PROBLEM
Optimization is the easy part and the dangerous part. A search powerful enough to find an edge is powerful enough to fit noise — so the pipeline is built around the holdout, not the optimizer.

APPROACH
Strategy-file mode: drop in any strategy with entry/exit functions; it computes indicators, optimizes tunable params with walk-forward, stress-tests, and reports on a 25% holdout the optimizer never touched.
Discovery mode: describe a concept in plain English and it searches thousands of indicator / exit / regime combinations.
v3.0 ensemble: 6 structurally distinct strategies combined by risk-parity weighting under a volatility-regime overlay, validated through per-strategy CPCV, portfolio-level CPCV, and walk-forward weighting.

WHAT I LEARNED
A research tool should make it easy to disprove yourself. The honest headline number comes from the data the search was forbidden to touch.
HONEST LIMITATIONS
It is a research and screening tool, not a turnkey trading system — surviving the pipeline earns a candidate a paper deployment, nothing more.

Automated 0DTE Options Bots
algorithmic-options-trading-system
Automated 0DTE options strategies on SPY / QQQ / SPX, built on the Option Alpha no-code platform and run on a $125K paper portfolio. Three bots, with VIX filters, entry windows, position caps, and a mandatory time-exit.
PAPER • SMALL SAMPLE
Reported paper results (Feb 2026): about +$16,000 (≈ +12.8% on the paper account) across 118 closed trades, with under 3% max drawdown.
HONEST FRAMING
I include this on purpose, framed honestly. These are paper, small-sample numbers with the signature of a short-volatility profile — the kind of result that looks perfect right up until a tail event erases it. It is not a proven edge. It is the experiment that taught me about tail risk and overfitting, and it is exactly why I built the guilty-until-proven-innocent methodology behind everything above.

A Dockerized, tested Python project exploring an automated, multi-agent 'AI hedge fund' workflow. Where it builds on an open-source framework, attribution belongs in the write-up.

A tiered automation tool for options workflows: webhooks, then Playwright browser automation, then computer-use — escalating only as far as a task requires.
Content-automation-engine
A social-media content-automation system with real infrastructure — Grafana, a database, migrations. The architecture is the point, not the file count.

I grew up watching my father trade and took away one lesson early: results are a byproduct of process — define your edge, manage your risk, and stay level-headed when the noise gets loud. I've spent the last few years turning that instinct into real work: algorithmic strategies on QuantConnect, a research pipeline that stress-tests ideas until most of them break, and a habit of documenting both what survived and what didn't.Away from the screen I run cross country, wrestle, study Mandarin, and shoot photography and drone film. Mengzi taught me that judgment is cultivated, not innate. The Gita taught me to act with discipline and detach from the result. Mill keeps me weighing consequences and staying open to being wrong; Hegel frames engineering as the reconciliation of competing constraints; the Dhammapada treats a well-directed mind as a technical asset. secText.about:
01 • ABOUT
A builder of quantitative systems.
I'm Aryan Sharma, a high-school student in the Washington, D.C. area who builds and validates quantitative trading systems. I grew up watching my father trade and took away one lesson early: results are a byproduct of process — define your edge, manage your risk, and stay level-headed when the noise gets loud. I've spent the last few years turning that instinct into real work: algorithmic strategies on QuantConnect, a research pipeline that stress-tests ideas until most of them break, and a habit of documenting both what survived and what didn't.
Away from the screen I run cross country, wrestle, study Mandarin, and shoot photography and drone film. The same temperament runs through all of it — and a quieter thread of moral philosophy runs underneath, shaping how I think about the systems I build.
ON METHOD
I read moral philosophy and let it shape how I engineer. Mengzi taught me that judgment is cultivated, not innate. The Gita taught me to act with discipline and detach from the result. Mill keeps me weighing consequences and staying open to being wrong; Hegel frames engineering as the reconciliation of competing constraints; the Dhammapada treats a well-directed mind as a technical asset. None of it is decoration — it is why I care whether the systems I build are honest about their limits.
JACK’S COMPASS — IT POINTS TO WHAT YOU WANT MOST
,
PIRATES OF THE CARIBBEAN
01 • NW
Process over outcome
I judge my work by the parts I control — preparation, discipline, honest effort — not by the scoreboard. It is an idea I borrow from the Bhagavad Gita: do your duty well, and hold the result loosely.
02 • NE
Intellectual honesty
I treat every backtest as guilty until proven innocent. The work I am proudest of is not a winning strategy — it is the documented graveyard of my own ideas that did not survive testing.
03 • SW
A cross-cultural lens
Six years of Mandarin and a childhood spent traveling taught me to question my assumptions and read a situation from more than one angle before acting on it.
04 • SE
An athlete's discipline
Wrestling, distance running, and trading taught me the same lesson in three arenas: define the edge, manage the risk, and trust that small, repeated improvements compound.

05 • FLAGSHIP · 161 FILES
Automated Strategy Research Pipeline
Optuna-Screener
A Python pipeline that discovers, optimizes, and validates strategies on real market data and answers one question honestly: does this work on data it has never seen?
THE PROBLEM
Optimization is the easy part and the dangerous part. A search powerful enough to find an edge is powerful enough to fit noise — so the pipeline is built around the holdout, not the optimizer.
FIG. 2 • OPTUNA-SCREENER • 6 STAGES • 1 BRANCH

NEVER OPTIMIZED ON

V3.0 ENSEMBLE
RISK-PARITY WEIGHTING • PER-STRATEGY + PORTFOLIO CPCV
APPROACH
Strategy-file mode: drop in any strategy with entry/exit functions; it computes indicators, optimizes tunable params with walk-forward, stress-tests, and reports on a 25% holdout the optimizer never touched.
Discovery mode: describe a concept in plain English and it searches thousands of indicator / exit / regime combinations.
v3.0 ensemble: 6 structurally distinct strategies combined by risk-parity weighting under a volatility-regime overlay, validated through per-strategy CPCV, portfolio-level CPCV, and walk-forward weighting.
MONTE-CARLO SHUFFLES
3,000+
trade-sequence resampling
OUT-OF-SAMPLE HOLDOUT
25%
optimizer never sees it
TARGET CPCV SHARPE
1.0–1.5
anything > 2.0 is a red flag
WHAT I LEARNED
A research tool should make it easy to disprove yourself. The honest headline number comes from the data the search was forbidden to touch.
HONEST LIMITATIONS
It is a research and screening tool, not a turnkey trading system — surviving the pipeline earns a candidate a paper deployment, nothing more.

WHERE THE DISCIPLINE STARTED
Automated 0DTE Options Bots
algorithmic-options-trading-system
Automated 0DTE options strategies on SPY / QQQ / SPX, built on the Option Alpha no-code platform and run on a $125K paper portfolio. Three bots, with VIX filters, entry windows, position caps, and a mandatory time-exit.
PAPER • SMALL SAMPLE
Reported paper results (Feb 2026): about +$16,000 (≈ +12.8% on the paper account) across 118 closed trades, with under 3% max drawdown.
HONEST FRAMING
I include this on purpose, framed honestly. These are paper, small-sample numbers with the signature of a short-volatility profile — the kind of result that looks perfect right up until a tail event erases it. It is not a proven edge. It is the experiment that taught me about tail risk and overfitting, and it is exactly why I built the guilty-until-proven-innocent methodology behind everything above.
SUPPORTING WORK

A Dockerized, tested Python project exploring an automated, multi-agent 'AI hedge fund' workflow. Where it builds on an open-source framework, attribution belongs in the write-up.

An 82-file Python data pipeline on a clean adapter pattern (Apify, CSV) with scheduled runs and a weekly email digest — a straightforward data-engineering example.
Options-claw
A tiered automation tool for options workflows: webhooks, then Playwright browser automation, then computer-use — escalating only as far as a task requires.
Content-automation-engine
A social-media content-automation system with real infrastructure — Grafana, a database, migrations. The architecture is the point, not the file count.

01
Cultivate judgment
Good judgment is trained, not issued at birth. I treat skill and temperament like mileage or lifts — built slowly, on purpose.
AFTER MENGZI
YOU
02
Act, then release the result
Do the work well and hold the outcome loosely. The scoreboard is feedback, not a verdict on the process that produced it.
AFTER THE BHAGAVAD GITA
YOU
03
Weigh the consequences
Systems that touch people carry downstream effects. Risk is partly a moral category — and staying open to being wrong is part of the design.
AFTER J. S. MILL
YOU
04
Synthesize the constraints
Engineering is the reconciliation of competing demands — speed against cost, ambition against honesty. Progress comes through that tension, not around it.
AFTER HEGEL
YOU
05
Attend carefully
A disciplined, well-directed mind is a technical asset. Most failures I have seen were failures of attention before they were failures of math.

secAll.about: 01 • AboutA builder of quantitative systems.JACK’S COMPASS — IT POINTS TO WHAT YOU WANT MOST• , PIRATES OF THE CARIBBEANI'm Aryan Sharma, a high-school student in the Washington, D.C. area who builds and validates quantitative trading systems. I grew up watching my father trade and took away one lesson early: results are a byproduct of process — define your edge, manage your risk, and stay level-headed when the noise gets loud. I've spent the last few years turning that instinct into real work: algorithmic strategies on QuantConnect, a research pipeline that stress-tests ideas until most of them break, and a habit of documenting both what survived and what didn't.Away from the screen I run cross country, wrestle, study Mandarin, and shoot photography and drone film. The same temperament runs through all of it — and a quieter thread of moral philosophy runs underneath, shaping how I think about the systems I build.On methodI read moral philosophy and let it shape how I engineer. Mengzi taught me that judgment is cultivated, not innate. The Gita taught me to act with discipline and detach from the result. Mill keeps me weighing consequences and staying open to being wrong; Hegel frames engineering as the reconciliation of competing constraints; the Dhammapada treats a well-directed mind as a technical asset. None of it is decoration — it is why I care whether the systems I build are honest about their limits.JACK’S COMPASS — IT POINTS TO WHAT YOU WANT MOST• , PIRATES OF THE CARIBBEAN01 • NWProcess over outcomeI judge my work by the parts I control — preparation, discipline, honest effort — not by the scoreboard. It is an idea I borrow from the Bhagavad Gita: do your duty well, and hold the result loosely.02 • NEIntellectual honestyI treat every backtest as guilty until proven innocent. The work I am proudest of is not a winning strategy — it is the documented graveyard of my own ideas that did not survive testing.03 • SWA cross-cultural lensSix years of Mandarin and a childhood spent traveling taught me to question my assumptions and read a situation from more than one angle before acting on it.04 • SEAn athlete's disciplineWrestling, distance running, and trading taught me the same lesson in three arenas: define the edge, manage the risk, and trust that small, repeated improvements compound.

secAll.optuna-screener: What is a machine?“A machine is anything that reduces human effort.” — , RanchoWHAT IS A MACHINE?• , 3 IDIOTS05 • Flagship · 161 filesAutomated Strategy Research PipelineOptuna-ScreenerA Python pipeline that discovers, optimizes, and validates strategies on real market data and answers one question honestly: does this work on data it has never seen?The problemOptimization is the easy part and the dangerous part. A search powerful enough to find an edge is powerful enough to fit noise — so the pipeline is built around the holdout, not the optimizer.FIG. 2 • Optuna-Screener • 6 stages • 1 branchStrategy file / discoveryentry_fn • exit_fnIndicatorscomputed per strategyOptuna TPEwalk-forwardStress testsMonte Carlo • noise25% holdoutnever optimized onReportPlotly HTMLv3.0 ensemblerisk-parity weighting • per-strategy + portfolio CPCVStrategy file / discoveryentry_fn • exit_fnIndicatorscomputed per strategyOptuna TPEwalk-forwardStress testsMonte Carlo • noise25% holdoutnever optimized onReportPlotly HTMLv3.0 ensemblerisk-parity weighting • per-strategy + portfolio CPCVApproachStrategy-file mode: drop in any strategy with entry/exit functions; it computes indicators, optimizes tunable params with walk-forward, stress-tests, and reports on a 25% holdout the optimizer never touched.Discovery mode: describe a concept in plain English and it searches thousands of indicator / exit / regime combinations.v3.0 ensemble: 6 structurally distinct strategies combined by risk-parity weighting under a volatility-regime overlay, validated through per-strategy CPCV, portfolio-level CPCV, and walk-forward weighting.Monte-Carlo shuffles3,000+trade-sequence resamplingOut-of-sample holdout25%optimizer never sees itTarget CPCV Sharpe1.0–1.5anything > 2.0 is a red flagWhat I learnedA research tool should make it easy to disprove yourself. The honest headline number comes from the data the search was forbidden to touch.Honest limitationsIt is a research and screening tool, not a turnkey trading system — surviving the pipeline earns a candidate a paper deployment, nothing more.Stack • Python 3.11+ · Optuna (TPE) · Pandas / NumPy · Polygon.io API · Plotly · MIT-licensed[ chart slot — drop a real exported equity curve / report here ]Where the discipline startedAutomated 0DTE Options Botsalgorithmic-options-trading-systemAutomated 0DTE options strategies on SPY / QQQ / SPX, built on the Option Alpha no-code platform and run on a $125K paper portfolio. Three bots, with VIX filters, entry windows, position caps, and a mandatory time-exit.Paper • small sampleReported paper results (Feb 2026): about +$16,000 (≈ +12.8% on the paper account) across 118 closed trades, with under 3% max drawdown.Honest framingI include this on purpose, framed honestly. These are paper, small-sample numbers with the signature of a short-volatility profile — the kind of result that looks perfect right up until a tail event erases it. It is not a proven edge. It is the experiment that taught me about tail risk and overfitting, and it is exactly why I built the guilty-until-proven-innocent methodology behind everything above.Supporting workTools, pipelines, automation.Hedge-fundA Dockerized, tested Python project exploring an automated, multi-agent 'AI hedge fund' workflow. Where it builds on an open-source framework, attribution belongs in the write-up.Data-ScraperAn 82-file Python data pipeline on a clean adapter pattern (Apify, CSV) with scheduled runs and a weekly email digest — a straightforward data-engineering example.Options-clawA tiered automation tool for options workflows: webhooks, then Playwright browser automation, then computer-use — escalating only as far as a task requires.Content-automation-engineA social-media content-automation system with real infrastructure — Grafana, a database, migrations. The architecture is the point, not the file count.Also on GitHub Options-plan- (early / idea-stage) • -ai-vids (early / idea-stage)

A builder of quantitative systems.
I'm Aryan Sharma, a high-school student in the Washington, D.C. area who builds and validates quantitative trading systems. I grew up watching my father trade and took away one lesson early: results are a byproduct of process — define your edge, manage your risk, and stay level-headed when the noise gets loud. I've spent the last few years turning that instinct into real work: algorithmic strategies on QuantConnect, a research pipeline that stress-tests ideas until most of them break, and a habit of documenting both what survived and what didn't.
Away from the screen I run cross country, wrestle, study Mandarin, and shoot photography and drone film. The same temperament runs through all of it — and a quieter thread of moral philosophy runs underneath, shaping how I think about the systems I build.
ON METHOD
I read moral philosophy and let it shape how I engineer. Mengzi taught me that judgment is cultivated, not innate. The Gita taught me to act with discipline and detach from the result. Mill keeps me weighing consequences and staying open to being wrong; Hegel frames engineering as the reconciliation of competing constraints; the Dhammapada treats a well-directed mind as a technical asset. None of it is decoration — it is why I care whether the systems I build are honest about their limits.

Automated Strategy Research Pipeline
Optuna-Screener
A Python pipeline that discovers, optimizes, and validates strategies on real market data and answers one question honestly: does this work on data it has never seen?
THE PROBLEM
Optimization is the easy part and the dangerous part. A search powerful enough to find an edge is powerful enough to fit noise — so the pipeline is built around the holdout, not the optimizer.

APPROACH
Strategy-file mode: drop in any strategy with entry/exit functions; it computes indicators, optimizes tunable params with walk-forward, stress-tests, and reports on a 25% holdout the optimizer never touched.
Discovery mode: describe a concept in plain English and it searches thousands of indicator / exit / regime combinations.
v3.0 ensemble: 6 structurally distinct strategies combined by risk-parity weighting under a volatility-regime overlay, validated through per-strategy CPCV, portfolio-level CPCV, and walk-forward weighting.

HONEST LIMITATIONS
It is a research and screening tool, not a turnkey trading system — surviving the pipeline earns a candidate a paper deployment, nothing more.

WHERE THE DISCIPLINE STARTED
Automated 0DTE Options Bots
algorithmic-options-trading-system
Automated 0DTE options strategies on SPY / QQQ / SPX, built on the Option Alpha no-code platform and run on a $125K paper portfolio. Three bots, with VIX filters, entry windows, position caps, and a mandatory time-exit.
PAPER • SMALL SAMPLE
Reported paper results (Feb 2026): about +$16,000 (≈ +12.8% on the paper account) across 118 closed trades, with under 3% max drawdown.
HONEST FRAMING
I include this on purpose, framed honestly. These are paper, small-sample numbers with the signature of a short-volatility profile — the kind of result that looks perfect right up until a tail event erases it. It is not a proven edge. It is the experiment that taught me about tail risk and overfitting, and it is exactly why I built the guilty-until-proven-innocent methodology behind everything above.

Cultivate judgment
Good judgment is trained, not issued at birth. I treat skill and temperament like mileage or lifts — built slowly, on purpose.

Act, then release the result
Do the work well and hold the outcome loosely. The scoreboard is feedback, not a verdict on the process that produced it.
AFTER THE BHAGAVAD GITA
YOU
03
Weigh the consequences
Systems that touch people carry downstream effects. Risk is partly a moral category — and staying open to being wrong is part of the design.
AFTER J. S. MILL
YOU
04
Synthesize the constraints
Engineering is the reconciliation of competing demands — speed against cost, ambition against honesty. Progress comes through that tension, not around it.

Attend carefully
A disciplined, well-directed mind is a technical asset. Most failures I have seen were failures of attention before they were failures of math.

secText.about:
01 • ABOUT
A builder of quantitative systems.
I'm Aryan Sharma, a high-school student in the Washington, D.C. area who builds and validates quantitative trading systems. I grew up watching my father trade and took away one lesson early: results are a byproduct of process — define your edge, manage your risk, and stay level-headed when the noise gets loud. I've spent the last few years turning that instinct into real work: algorithmic strategies on QuantConnect, a research pipeline that stress-tests ideas until most of them break, and a habit of documenting both what survived and what didn't.
Away from the screen I run cross country, wrestle, study Mandarin, and shoot photography and drone film. The same temperament runs through all of it — and a quieter thread of moral philosophy runs underneath, shaping how I think about the systems I build.
ON METHOD
I read moral philosophy and let it shape how I engineer. Mengzi taught me that judgment is cultivated, not innate. The Gita taught me to act with discipline and detach from the result. Mill keeps me weighing consequences and staying open to being wrong; Hegel frames engineering as the reconciliation of competing constraints; the Dhammapada treats a well-directed mind as a technical asset. None of it is decoration — it is why I care whether the systems I build are honest about their limits.
JACK’S COMPASS — IT POINTS TO WHAT YOU WANT MOST
,
PIRATES OF THE CARIBBEAN
01 • NW
Process over outcome
I judge my work by the parts I control — preparation, discipline, honest effort — not by the scoreboard. It is an idea I borrow from the Bhagavad Gita: do your duty well, and hold the result loosely.
02 • NE
Intellectual honesty
I treat every backtest as guilty until proven innocent. The work I am proudest of is not a winning strategy — it is the documented graveyard of my own ideas that did not survive testing.
03 • SW
A cross-cultural lens
Six years of Mandarin and a childhood spent traveling taught me to question my assumptions and read a situation from more than one angle before acting on it.
04 • SE
An athlete's discipline
Wrestling, distance running, and trading taught me the same lesson in three arenas: define the edge, manage the risk, and trust that small, repeated improvements compound.

Discovery mode: describe a concept in plain English and it searches thousands of indicator / exit / regime combinations.

WHAT I LEARNED
A research tool should make it easy to disprove yourself. The honest headline number comes from the data the search was forbidden to touch.

HONEST FRAMING
I include this on purpose, framed honestly. These are paper, small-sample numbers with the signature of a short-volatility profile — the kind of result that looks perfect right up until a tail event erases it. It is not a proven edge. It is the experiment that taught me about tail risk and overfitting, and it is exactly why I built the guilty-until-proven-innocent methodology behind everything above.

THE MAP OF THE PRINCIPLES
10 • PRINCIPLES
A small philosophy of work.
Five ideas I actually use when I build. The names are sources, not decoration.
THE MARAUDER’S MAP
,
HARRY POTTER
YOU
01
Cultivate judgment
Good judgment is trained, not issued at birth. I treat skill and temperament like mileage or lifts — built slowly, on purpose.
AFTER MENGZI
YOU
02
Act, then release the result
Do the work well and hold the outcome loosely. The scoreboard is feedback, not a verdict on the process that produced it.
AFTER THE BHAGAVAD GITA
YOU
03
Weigh the consequences
Systems that touch people carry downstream effects. Risk is partly a moral category — and staying open to being wrong is part of the design.
AFTER J. S. MILL
YOU
04
Synthesize the constraints
Engineering is the reconciliation of competing demands — speed against cost, ambition against honesty. Progress comes through that tension, not around it.
AFTER HEGEL
YOU
05
Attend carefully
A disciplined, well-directed mind is a technical asset. Most failures I have seen were failures of attention before they were failures of math.

01 • ABOUT
A builder of quantitative systems.
I'm Aryan Sharma, a high-school student in the Washington, D.C. area who builds and validates quantitative trading systems. I grew up watching my father trade and took away one lesson early: results are a byproduct of process — define your edge, manage your risk, and stay level-headed when the noise gets loud. I've spent the last few years turning that instinct into real work: algorithmic strategies on QuantConnect, a research pipeline that stress-tests ideas until most of them break, and a habit of documenting both what survived and what didn't.
Away from the screen I run cross country, wrestle, study Mandarin, and shoot photography and drone film. The same temperament runs through all of it — and a quieter thread of moral philosophy runs underneath, shaping how I think about the systems I build.
ON METHOD
I read moral philosophy and let it shape how I engineer. Mengzi taught me that judgment is cultivated, not innate. The Gita taught me to act with discipline and detach from the result. Mill keeps me weighing consequences and staying open to being wrong; Hegel frames engineering as the reconciliation of competing constraints; the Dhammapada treats a well-directed mind as a technical asset. None of it is decoration — it is why I care whether the systems I build are honest about their limits.
JACK’S COMPASS — IT POINTS TO WHAT YOU WANT MOST

Process over outcome
I judge my work by the parts I control — preparation, discipline, honest effort — not by the scoreboard. It is an idea I borrow from the Bhagavad Gita: do your duty well, and hold the result loosely.

Intellectual honesty
I treat every backtest as guilty until proven innocent. The work I am proudest of is not a winning strategy — it is the documented graveyard of my own ideas that did not survive testing.

Six years of Mandarin and a childhood spent traveling taught me to question my assumptions and read a situation from more than one angle before acting on it.

An athlete's discipline
Wrestling, distance running, and trading taught me the same lesson in three arenas: define the edge, manage the risk, and trust that small, repeated improvements compound.

Optuna-Screener
A Python pipeline that discovers, optimizes, and validates strategies on real market data and answers one question honestly: does this work on data it has never seen?
THE PROBLEM
Optimization is the easy part and the dangerous part. A search powerful enough to find an edge is powerful enough to fit noise — so the pipeline is built around the holdout, not the optimizer.

APPROACH
Strategy-file mode: drop in any strategy with entry/exit functions; it computes indicators, optimizes tunable params with walk-forward, stress-tests, and reports on a 25% holdout the optimizer never touched.
Discovery mode: describe a concept in plain English and it searches thousands of indicator / exit / regime combinations.
v3.0 ensemble: 6 structurally distinct strategies combined by risk-parity weighting under a volatility-regime overlay, validated through per-strategy CPCV, portfolio-level CPCV, and walk-forward weighting.

WHAT I LEARNED
A research tool should make it easy to disprove yourself. The honest headline number comes from the data the search was forbidden to touch.
HONEST LIMITATIONS
It is a research and screening tool, not a turnkey trading system — surviving the pipeline earns a candidate a paper deployment, nothing more.

Automated 0DTE options strategies on SPY / QQQ / SPX, built on the Option Alpha no-code platform and run on a $125K paper portfolio. Three bots, with VIX filters, entry windows, position caps, and a mandatory time-exit.
PAPER • SMALL SAMPLE
Reported paper results (Feb 2026): about +$16,000 (≈ +12.8% on the paper account) across 118 closed trades, with under 3% max drawdown.
HONEST FRAMING
I include this on purpose, framed honestly. These are paper, small-sample numbers with the signature of a short-volatility profile — the kind of result that looks perfect right up until a tail event erases it. It is not a proven edge. It is the experiment that taught me about tail risk and overfitting, and it is exactly why I built the guilty-until-proven-innocent methodology behind everything above.

I grew up watching my father trade and took away one lesson early: results are a byproduct of process — define your edge, manage your risk, and stay level-headed when the noise gets loud. secText.about:
01 • ABOUT
A builder of quantitative systems.
I'm Aryan Sharma, a high-school student in the Washington, D.C. area who builds and validates quantitative trading systems. I grew up watching my father trade and took away one lesson early: results are a byproduct of process — define your edge, manage your risk, and stay level-headed when the noise gets loud. I've spent the last few years turning that instinct into real work: algorithmic strategies on QuantConnect, a research pipeline that stress-tests ideas until most of them break, and a habit of documenting both what survived and what didn't.
Away from the screen I run cross country, wrestle, study Mandarin, and shoot photography and drone film. The same temperament runs through all of it — and a quieter thread of moral philosophy runs underneath, shaping how I think about the systems I build.
ON METHOD
I read moral philosophy and let it shape how I engineer. Mengzi taught me that judgment is cultivated, not innate. The Gita taught me to act with discipline and detach from the result. Mill keeps me weighing consequences and staying open to being wrong; Hegel frames engineering as the reconciliation of competing constraints; the Dhammapada treats a well-directed mind as a technical asset. None of it is decoration — it is why I care whether the systems I build are honest about their limits.
JACK’S COMPASS — IT POINTS TO WHAT YOU WANT MOST
,
PIRATES OF THE CARIBBEAN
01 • NW
Process over outcome
I judge my work by the parts I control — preparation, discipline, honest effort — not by the scoreboard. It is an idea I borrow from the Bhagavad Gita: do your duty well, and hold the result loosely.
02 • NE
Intellectual honesty
I treat every backtest as guilty until proven innocent. The work I am proudest of is not a winning strategy — it is the documented graveyard of my own ideas that did not survive testing.
03 • SW
A cross-cultural lens
Six years of Mandarin and a childhood spent traveling taught me to question my assumptions and read a situation from more than one angle before acting on it.
04 • SE
An athlete's discipline
Wrestling, distance running, and trading taught me the same lesson in three arenas: define the edge, manage the risk, and trust that small, repeated improvements compound.

05 • FLAGSHIP · 161 FILES
Automated Strategy Research Pipeline
Optuna-Screener
A Python pipeline that discovers, optimizes, and validates strategies on real market data and answers one question honestly: does this work on data it has never seen?
THE PROBLEM
Optimization is the easy part and the dangerous part. A search powerful enough to find an edge is powerful enough to fit noise — so the pipeline is built around the holdout, not the optimizer.
FIG. 2 • OPTUNA-SCREENER • 6 STAGES • 1 BRANCH

INDICATORS
